title: Building Estandarte in Godot with AI coding assistance: validating a villager economy and baking pixel art
author: SouthernReach143
selftext:
I'm Diego, developing Estandarte, a medieval RTS for Android in Godot 4/GDScript under One Week Games. I've used substantial AI coding assistance, and wanted to share a concrete part of the workflow: checking the economy's state transitions instead of judging generated code by how plausible it looks.

Villagers physically carry food, wood, gold and stone to the appropriate depots. A new work order has to coexist with a load already being carried. One example in the project's economy-order test sets a worker's cargo to seven wood, then assigns that worker to gold. It checks that the wood is preserved and delivered first, that the wood balance increases by seven while the gold balance stays unchanged, and that the worker then resumes the new job with the right tool. The same suite checks that saving and loading preserves jobs and delivered-resource totals. These are concrete simulation assertions, separate from checking whether the touch interface feels usable.

The art workflow has also changed during development. The current gameplay pixel sprites come from GDScript drawing code baked into RGBA atlases, rather than pixelating the earlier illustrations. Earlier illustrated assets and reference experiments used image generation too, so I want to be clear about both kinds of AI involvement.

Estandarte currently has six civilizations, four ages, an offline campaign and online modes. It's still in closed Android testing; public pre-registration has no confirmed date. The store page may only be visible to enrolled testers for now.

For developers using AI on simulation-heavy games, which worker-order or resource-conservation invariants do you write regression checks for first? I'm especially interested in reassignment while a unit is carrying resources and in save/load consistency.

Project store page: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.estandarte.valle
